question.text:
Consider the function $L: \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}   \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined by $L(\mathbf{A}) = \dfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b})^T(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}),$ where
\[
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 10 \\ 20 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
What is $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L$ at 
$
\mathbf{A}  =  \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}?
$
question.freeAnswerChoice:
$\nabla_{\mathbf{A}}= \:\:$ [ answer: 0; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ] [ answer: 130; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ] [ answer: 260; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ]
$0$ [ answer: -80; type: number; width: 35; margin-left: 4; margin-right: 4; ] $-160$
question.explanation:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $\mathbf{A}$ is a matrix of the same shape as $\mathbf{A}$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by \[ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}, \] the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $\mathbf{A}.$

We can compute $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Then, $L(\mathbf{A}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{y}$ and

\[ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}} = \sum_{k=1}^2 \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}} \]

Now, since \[ \nabla_{\mathbf{y}} L = \nabla_{\mathbf{y}} \bigg( \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{y} \bigg) = \mathbf{y}, \]

we have that

\[ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} = y_k. \]

Writing out $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}$ in component-wise notation as \[ y_i = \sum\limits_{j=1}^3 a_{ij}x_j - b_i, \] we have

  • $\dfrac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}} = x_j$ if $i = k$, and

  • $\dfrac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}} = 0$ if $i \neq k.$

This means that

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}} &= \sum_{k=1}^2 \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial y_i} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_i}{\partial a_{ij}} \\[5pt] &= y_i \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_i}{\partial a_{ij}} \\[5pt] &= y_i x_j. \end{align*}

The $(i,j)$th entry of $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L$ is the $i$th entry of $\mathbf{y}$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $\mathbf{x}$, so

\[ \nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T. \]

Finally, evaluating $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L$ at $\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},$ we get

\begin{align*} \nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L &= \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T \\[5pt] &= \left(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\right) \cdot \mathbf{x}^T \\[5pt] &= \left(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 10 \\ 20 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}\right) \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 10 & 20 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \left(\begin{bmatrix} 20 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}\right) \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 10 & 20 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 13 \\ -8 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 10 & 20 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{0}} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{130}} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{260}} \\ 0 & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{{-80}} & -160 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the function $L: \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined by $L(\mathbf{A}) = 2\left(\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\right)$ where \[ \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}. \] What is $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L$ at $ \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}? $
question.explanation:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $\mathbf{A}$ is a matrix of the same shape as $\mathbf{A}$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by \[ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}, \] the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $\mathbf{A}.$

Writing out $L$ in component-wise notation as \[ L = \sum\limits_{i=1}^2 \sum\limits_{j=1}^3 2 a_{ij} y_i x_j, \] we have \[ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}} = 2 y_i x_j. \]

Thus, $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L = 2\left(\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T\right).$

Evaluating at the given values $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix},$ we get

\[ \nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L = 2\left(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\right) = 2\left(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 14 & -7 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\right) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 & 0 \\ 28 & -14 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.explanation:

Writing out $L$ in component-wise notation as \[ L = \sum\limits_{i=1}^2 \sum\limits_{j=1}^3 a_{ij} y_i x_j, \] we have \[ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}} = y_i x_j. \]

Evaluating at the given values $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix},$ we get

question.text: Consider the function $L: \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined by $L(\mathbf{A}) = \mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ where \[ \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}. \] What is $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L$ at $ \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 6 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}? $
question.explanation:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $\mathbf{A}$ is a matrix of the same shape as $\mathbf{A}$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by \[ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}, \] the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $\mathbf{A}.$

Writing out $L$ in component-wise notation as \[ L = \sum\limits_{i=1}^3 \sum\limits_{j=1}^2 a_{ij} y_i x_j, \] we have \[ \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}} = y_i x_j. \]

Thus, $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T.$

Evaluating at the given values $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 4 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix},$ we get
